title: Is Anything Truly Random?
question: When we call a dice roll or a radioactive decay random, do we mean something is genuinely uncaused, or only that we lack the knowledge to predict it?
summary: An exploration of the difference between randomness born of ignorance and randomness that may be woven into the fabric of reality itself, from tumbling dice to quantum measurement to the mathematics of incompressible strings.
content:
A coin flip feels random, but it isn't, not really. If you knew the coin's exact velocity, spin, air resistance, and the force of your thumb, physics would let you predict heads or tails every time. Casinos and dice games run on this kind of "randomness," which is really just complexity that outpaces our ability to track it. Physicists call this epistemic randomness: uncertainty that lives in our heads, not in the world. The far stranger question is whether any randomness is not like this, whether some events are uncaused all the way down.

The Quantum Complication

Quantum mechanics is the leading candidate for genuine, ontological randomness. When a radioactive atom decays, or a photon passes through a polarizing filter, standard quantum theory says there is no hidden fact determining the outcome in advance, only a probability. For decades, physicists like Einstein suspected this was incompleteness rather than true chance, hoping some undiscovered "hidden variable" would restore determinism. John Bell's theorem, later confirmed experimentally, closed off the most natural version of that hope: any hidden-variable theory matching quantum predictions must abandon locality, meaning influences that seem to act faster than light. Most physicists now accept that quantum outcomes are, as far as any experiment can tell, irreducibly random.

A Different Definition, From Mathematics

Mathematicians offer a completely different way to define randomness that has nothing to do with physics: algorithmic randomness. A string of digits is called random if no computer program shorter than the string itself can generate it, meaning the string cannot be compressed or described more briefly than just writing it out. By this definition, almost every real number is random, since only a vanishingly small fraction can be produced by short programs. Yet, strangely, we can never definitively prove that any specific number we write down is random in this sense; the concept guarantees randomness is common while making it almost impossible to certify in any particular case.

Why the Distinction Matters

The difference between epistemic and ontological randomness isn't just philosophical hair-splitting. It bears on free will (is unpredictability in the brain evidence of freedom, or just noise?), on cryptography (a random number generator that is secretly predictable is a catastrophic security hole), and on how we interpret the universe itself. A deterministic universe that merely looks random to limited observers is a very different place than one with true, uncaused branching at its foundation. Interestingly, some interpretations of quantum mechanics, like the many-worlds view, restore determinism at the cost of saying every outcome happens somewhere, just not in the branch you experience.

Living With Uncertainty

In practice, we rarely need to resolve this question to function. Casinos, cryptographers, and statisticians treat "good enough" unpredictability as random and move on. But the deeper puzzle, whether the universe ever truly rolls dice or whether every outcome was fixed since the Big Bang and we simply cannot see the strings, remains one of the most unresolved questions at the intersection of physics, mathematics, and philosophy.

perspectives.title: Physics Perspective
perspectives.description: Bell's theorem and its experimental confirmations rule out local hidden-variable explanations for quantum outcomes, leaving genuine indeterminism as the standard interpretation, unless one accepts exotic alternatives like many-worlds or superdeterminism.

perspectives.title: Mathematics Perspective
perspectives.description: Algorithmic (Kolmogorov) randomness defines a string as random if it cannot be compressed into a shorter description, showing that almost all numbers are random even though no specific one can ever be proven so with certainty.

perspectives.title: Philosophy Perspective
perspectives.description: The distinction between epistemic randomness, arising from ignorance, and ontological randomness, arising from the nature of reality itself, shapes debates over free will, causation, and what it even means for an event to be uncaused.

perspectives.title: Cryptography and Computer Science Perspective
perspectives.description: Practical systems depend on distinguishing true entropy sources, like quantum noise or atmospheric static, from pseudorandom algorithms that merely look unpredictable, since an attacker who can predict a random number generator can break the security built on top of it.

openQuestions: Is quantum randomness truly uncaused, or could some deeper layer of physics we haven't discovered restore determinism?
Can a fully deterministic universe still contain algorithmically random sequences, and if so, what would that even mean?
If most numbers are random in the mathematical sense, why does the physical universe appear so orderly and compressible at large scales?
Would proof that the universe is fundamentally random or fundamentally determined change how we think about moral responsibility?
